Onan
ō'nan
n. (second son of Judah, slain by the LORD for refusing his brother's widow the seed the duty required)
From Hebrew 'Onan, connected with 'on, strength or vigour, and by a homonym with sorrow. His name has been attached in later English to a sin the text does not principally charge him with.

Biblical Definition

Onan is the second son of Judah (Gen 38:4), and his whole history occupies three verses. When his elder brother Er was slain for wickedness, the duty of raising up seed to him fell on Onan, and Judah stated it plainly: “Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother” (Gen 38:8). Onan took the wife and refused the duty. The text is exact about his motive: “Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother” (Gen 38:9). He wanted the marriage without the obligation, the woman without the heir, and the inheritance undivided in his own line. It was calculated, repeated, and covetous. The verdict is one sentence: “And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also” (Gen 38:10). Two brothers dead by the hand of God in the space of six verses, in the household of the man through whom the Messiah would come — and the shocking thing is that the line survives at all. It survives through Tamar, whom both of them wronged.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Onan; in sacred history he is the second son of Judah, slain by the LORD for refusing to raise up seed to his brother.

expand to see more

ONAN, n. The second son of Judah by the daughter of Shua.

Upon the death of his elder brother Er, he was commanded to take Tamar and raise up seed to him.

He took her, but frustrated the purpose of the marriage, knowing the seed should not be his own.

The thing which he did displeased the LORD, and he was slain.

He died in the land of Canaan, before the going down into Egypt.

Key Scripture

Gen 38:4 — "And she conceived again, and bare a son; and she called his name Onan."

Gen 38:8 — "And Judah said unto Onan, Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother."

Gen 38:9 — "And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother."

Gen 38:10 — "And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also."

Modern Corruption

The passage is regularly reduced to a proof-text about one bodily act while the sin Scripture actually names — covetous refusal of a duty owed to the dead and to the defenceless — is passed over.

expand to see more

The English word coined from this man's name has narrowed the passage until most readers assume the mechanics were the offence. Moses is more precise. He gives the motive twice in one verse — Onan knew the seed should not be his, and acted lest he should give seed to his brother. The sin is a settled, repeated, self-interested refusal of a duty God had laid on him: to preserve a dead brother's name and to give a defenceless widow a place in Israel. He took the privileges of the marriage and withheld its purpose, which is fraud as well as covetousness. The dictionary does not thereby license what the passage has traditionally been used against; Scripture has much to say elsewhere about purity of body and mind, and “every one that looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Mat 5:28). It says only that a text should be made to say what it says.

The second corruption is the modern flinching at the verdict. God killed him, and readers want the sentence explained away as illness or coincidence. Genesis will not permit it: “the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also”. The God of Scripture is the living God who judges sin in real time when He pleases, as Ananias and Sapphira discovered in the age of grace itself (Act 5:5, 10). Modern religion has grown comfortable with a God who disapproves and does nothing. The Bible's God is holy, and the fear of Him is the beginning of wisdom: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb 10:31).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Onan (H209), Onan; yabam (H2992), to perform the brother-in-law's duty; zera' (H2233), seed; ra'a' (H7489), to be evil, displeasing; muth (H4191), to die, to be put to death.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Onan (H209) — Onan; the second son of Judah.

Hebrew yabam (H2992) — to perform the duty of a husband's brother; the obligation he refused.

Hebrew zera' (H2233) — seed, offspring; what he would not give to his brother's name.

Hebrew ra'a' (H7489) — to be evil, to displease; “the thing which he did displeased the LORD”.

Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to covet, desire; the root sin beneath the refusal, the inheritance kept whole.

Usage

"“Raise up seed to thy brother” — the duty stated in seven words."

"“Lest that he should give seed to his brother” — Moses gives the motive, not merely the act."

"“Wherefore he slew him also” — two brothers, six verses, one verdict."
